issues.legal_issue: A tenant who satisfies the statutory conditions for eviction for rent default is subject to a mandatory eviction decree, and the alternative protection for other cases does not apply.
material_facts: The eviction suit alleged rent payable monthly, arrears exceeding six months, service of a demand notice, and non-payment within the notice period.
The tenants did not dispute the standard rent or permitted increases within the relevant period.
The tenants paid neither the arrears within the notice period nor the amount required to avoid the statutory consequence under the applicable clause.
issues.conclusion: The statutory conditions for eviction were met, so the court was required to decree eviction; the alternative clause did not apply because it covered only cases outside the mandatory clause.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 12(2) and 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, the court must decree eviction when rent is payable monthly, there is no dispute about standard rent or permitted increases, arrears have continued for at least six months, and the tenant fails to pay within one month after notice. Section 12(3)(b), beginning with “In any other case,” applies only when clause (a) does not. The Court relied on Harbanslal Jagmohandas v. Prabhudas Shivlal, Jaywant S. Kulkarni v. Minochar Dosabhai Shroff, Ganpat Ladha v. Sashikant Vishnu Shinde, and Ganpat Ram Sharma v. Gayatri Devi.

rule.if: statutory_rent_eviction_suit and monthly_rent and arrears_for_at_least_six_months and no_rent_amount_dispute and notice_period_expired_without_payment

predicates.statutory_rent_eviction_suit: The landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction on a statutory ground of rent default.
predicates.monthly_rent: The tenant's rent was payable monthly.
predicates.arrears_for_at_least_six_months: The tenant had rent arrears lasting at least six months.
predicates.no_rent_amount_dispute: The tenant did not dispute the amount of standard rent or permitted increases during the relevant period.
predicates.notice_period_expired_without_payment: The tenant did not pay the demanded arrears before the notice period expired.
predicates.mandatory_eviction_decree_required: The court must decree eviction when the stated statutory rent-default conditions are met.

issues.definition: When a statutory rent-default eviction proceeding involves monthly rent, at least six months of arrears, no dispute about the rent amount, and non-payment within the notice period, the court must decree eviction.

issues.legal_issue: The power to do complete justice does not permit the court to disregard a mandatory statutory eviction requirement to benefit one party at the expense of the other.
material_facts: The tenants sought relief from eviction despite the finding that the mandatory statutory conditions for eviction had been satisfied.
Granting the requested relief would have deprived the landlord of the statutory right to an eviction decree.
issues.conclusion: Article 142 could not be used to relieve the tenants from the mandatory statutory consequence.
issues.legal_principle: Article 142 of the Constitution permits orders necessary for doing complete justice, but does not authorize the Court to ignore mandatory statutory provisions and thereby deny another party the benefit of those provisions. The Court distinguished Smt. Kamala Devi Budhia v. Hem Prabha Ganguli, where the remaining issue was procedural and did not affect substantive rights.

predicates.statutory_rent_eviction_suit: The proceeding seeks eviction under a statutory rent-control regime.
predicates.mandatory_statutory_eviction_conditions_: The facts satisfy a statutory rule requiring the court to order eviction.
predicates.relief_would_defeat_other_party_statutor: The requested relief would deprive the opposing party of a substantive right conferred by a mandatory statute.
predicates.complete_justice_power_cannot_override_m: The court cannot use its complete-justice power to set aside a mandatory statutory consequence to the opposing party's detriment.

issues.definition: When a statutory eviction rule mandates eviction and the requested relief would defeat the other party's statutory right, the complete-justice power cannot override that rule.

issues.legal_issue: Relief against forfeiture for non-payment of rent is unavailable when an eviction suit enforces a statutory rent-default right rather than a forfeiture of the lease.
material_facts: The landlord's suit relied on statutory rent-default provisions and did not claim that the lease had been forfeited under the law governing transfers of property.
The tenants sought relief against forfeiture based on their payment of rent after the suit began.
issues.conclusion: The tenants could not obtain relief under Section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act because the suit was not based on forfeiture of the lease.
issues.legal_principle: Section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, provides relief against forfeiture for non-payment of rent where a lease has been determined by forfeiture. Sections 111(g) and 114 concern forfeiture based on breach of an express condition permitting re-entry and the required notice. They do not apply where the landlord sues to enforce a statutory right arising from rent default. The Court considered Praduman Kumar v. Virendra Goyal.

predicates.rent_eviction_suit: The landlord brought a proceeding to evict a tenant for rent default.
predicates.claim_based_on_statutory_default_not_lea: The landlord relied on a statutory rent-default right rather than termination of the lease by forfeiture.
predicates.forfeiture_relief_unavailable: Relief against lease forfeiture cannot be granted in the proceeding.

issues.definition: Relief against forfeiture is unavailable when an eviction proceeding enforces a statutory rent-default right instead of a forfeiture of the lease.

issues.legal_issue: An amended rent-default protection does not apply retrospectively when the amendment provides no retrospective operation for that protection.
material_facts: The eviction suit was already pending when the rent-default provision was amended.
The amendment expressly gave retrospective effect to a different amended provision but did not do so for the rent-default provision.
The tenants sought the benefit of the amended protection for the existing proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The tenants could not claim the benefit of the amended rent-default provision in the pending suit because it was not retrospective.
issues.legal_principle: The amended Section 12(3) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, could not be given retrospective operation on its plain reading. The Court contrasted the express retrospective language used for the amendment to Section 15(2) with the absence of such language for Section 12(3), and held that the reopening provision in Section 25 did not enlarge the amended rent-default provision or remove the landlord's accrued statutory right.

predicates.rent_eviction_suit_pending_when_tenant_p: A rent-default eviction proceeding was pending when a tenant-protection provision was amended.
predicates.amendment_contains_no_retroactive_direct: The amendment did not state that the tenant protection applied retrospectively.
predicates.amended_tenant_protection_unavailable_fo: The amended tenant protection does not govern the earlier default in the pending proceeding.

issues.definition: If a rent-default eviction proceeding was pending when a tenant protection changed and the amendment did not make that change retrospective, the new protection does not apply to the earlier default.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory deposit deadline is the first day of the hearing or a court-fixed extension of that deadline, not any later date in the suit or appeal.
material_facts: The tenants deposited arrears after the date treated as the first day of the suit's hearing, relying on time allowed by the trial court.
The tenants also relied on later dates in the proceedings and on the reopening provision in the amending legislation.
The amended deposit requirement included interest that the tenants had not deposited.
issues.conclusion: A date fixed for settlement of issues may be treated as the first day of the hearing, while another date qualifies only as a court-fixed extension for an unavoidable reason; later dates in the suit or appeal and reopening proceedings do not create a new first day of hearing. The tenants also failed to meet the amended deposit requirement because they did not pay the required interest.
issues.legal_principle: The words “on the first day of the hearing of the suit or on or before such other date as the Court may fix” in Section 12(3) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, refer to the first hearing date or an extension fixed by the court when an unavoidable reason prevents deposit on that date. A date fixed for settlement of issues can be the first hearing date; other dates in a suit or appeal cannot be treated as further first hearing dates. Section 25 of the amending Act does not permit reopening to manufacture a new first hearing date. The Court relied on S.D. Chagan Lal v. Dalichand Virchand Shroff.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction under rent-control legislation with a statutory deposit deadline.
predicates.deposit_made_after_first_hearing: The tenant made the relevant deposit after the date that constituted the first day of the hearing.
predicates.no_valid_court_fixed_extension_for_that_: The court did not validly extend the deadline to cover the deposit date for an unavoidable reason.
predicates.deposit_does_not_satisfy_statutory_deadl: The later deposit does not satisfy the statutory timing requirement.

issues.definition: A deposit made after the first hearing does not meet the statutory deadline unless the court validly extended the time for an unavoidable reason.

issues.legal_issue: Relief under the law governing forfeiture of leases does not apply when a tenant's statutory rent default removes the bar to an eviction suit without forfeiting the lease.
material_facts: The landlord sued under statutory provisions governing rent default.
The statutory default removed the bar to the landlord's eviction suit and gave the landlord a right to seek an eviction decree.
The suit did not rely on an express lease condition allowing re-entry for non-payment of rent.
issues.conclusion: The tenants were not entitled to relief against forfeiture because no forfeiture of the lease was the basis of the suit.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 111(g) and 114 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, apply to forfeiture of a lease, including forfeiture for breach of an express condition permitting re-entry after the required notice. A statutory rent-default regime may remove a bar to an eviction action and confer a right to seek eviction without determining the lease by forfeiture.

predicates.eviction_suit: The landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.statutory_default_removes_bar_to_suit: The tenant's statutory default removed a legal bar to the landlord bringing the eviction proceeding.
predicates.lease_not_determined_by_forfeiture: The landlord did not establish that the lease had been determined by forfeiture.
predicates.transfer_of_property_forfeiture_relief_i: The tenant cannot obtain relief against forfeiture under the law governing leases.

issues.definition: When statutory default permits an eviction suit without determining the lease by forfeiture, relief against forfeiture is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord's pleading admission does not establish subletting against tenants who dispute it when the court requires the parties to prove their cases independently.
material_facts: The landlord pleaded that the tenants had sublet part of the premises to another occupant.
The tenants denied subletting and maintained that the occupant was a trespasser.
The occupant disputed that he was a subtenant and said he entered under an agreement with a tenant's son, who had no independent interest in the premises.
The parties presented evidence on their competing accounts.
issues.conclusion: The subletting issue had to be determined on evidence independently of the landlord's admission; the admission alone could not establish subletting against the tenants.
issues.legal_principle: Section 58 of the Evidence Act, 1872, generally recognizes judicial admissions, which stand on a higher footing than evidentiary admissions, but its proviso permits the court to require admitted facts to be proved otherwise. The Court relied on Nagindas Ramdas v. Dalpatram Ichharam and applied the proviso because the parties disputed the alleged subletting and the landlord's pleading could not itself resolve the dispute against the tenants.

rule.if: rental_property_dispute and landlord_pleads_subletting and tenants_deny_subletting and competing_parties_present_evidence

predicates.rental_property_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims about occupation of rented premises.
predicates.landlord_pleads_subletting: The landlord alleges in the pleadings that the tenants sublet part of the premises.
predicates.tenants_deny_subletting: The tenants deny that they sublet the premises and advance a contrary account of the occupant's status.
predicates.competing_parties_present_evidence: The parties provide evidence in support of their competing accounts.
predicates.subletting_must_be_proved_independently_: The alleged subletting must be established by evidence rather than by the landlord's admission alone.

issues.definition: When tenants contest a landlord's pleaded allegation of subletting and the parties provide competing evidence, the allegation must be proved independently of the landlord's admission.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court may interfere with a factual finding in writ review when the finding is arbitrary, unsupported by evidence, legally untenable, or contrary to a statutory provision or binding precedent.
material_facts: The lower courts found that the occupant was an illegal subtenant.
The occupant's own evidence said he entered under an agreement with a tenant's son, who had no independent interest in the premises, and he did not know who the tenants were.
The tenants denied subletting and presented evidence that the occupant was a trespasser.
The High Court set aside the lower courts' finding, and the Supreme Court concluded that no properly instructed court could have reached that finding on the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to set aside the finding of illegal subletting because it was not reasonably supported by the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Although factual findings are generally not interfered with in writ review, the rule has recognized exceptions, including where a finding is arbitrary, based on no evidence, legally untenable, or contrary to statute or binding precedent. The Court applied those exceptions to the finding that the occupant was an illegal subtenant.

predicates.writ_review_of_factual_finding: A writ proceeding challenges a factual finding made by a lower court.
predicates.finding_is_arbitrary_or_unsupported_or_l: The challenged finding is arbitrary, lacks evidentiary support, or is legally untenable.
predicates.reviewing_court_may_set_aside_factual_fi: The reviewing court may set aside the challenged factual finding.

issues.definition: In writ review, an arbitrary, unsupported, or legally untenable factual finding may be set aside.

issues.legal_issue: A person found to be a trespasser rather than a subtenant cannot claim protection given to qualifying subtenants under the amended rent legislation.
material_facts: The claimant sought the benefit of an amendment protecting certain subtenants who had entered possession and remained in possession on a specified date.
The High Court found that the claimant was a trespasser, not a subtenant.
The Supreme Court upheld that finding and therefore did not need to decide the separate questions about possession on the relevant date or the character of the writ proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The claimant could not obtain the amended subtenant protection because he was a trespasser rather than a subtenant.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, as amended, grants protection to qualifying subtenants, assignees, or transferees, not to a person found to be a trespasser. The Court did not decide the other grounds on which the High Court had rejected the claim.

predicates.claim_for_amended_subtenant_protection: A claimant seeks protection afforded by an amended provision to qualifying subtenants or transferees.
predicates.claimant_is_trespasser_not_subtenant: The claimant's occupation is found to be that of a trespasser rather than a subtenant.
predicates.amended_subtenant_protection_unavailable: The claimant cannot obtain the amended protection for subtenants.

issues.definition: A claimant found to be a trespasser rather than a subtenant cannot receive protection intended for qualifying subtenants.

issues.legal_issue: A court may continue hearing a matter after dictating a judgment if the judgment has not yet been delivered.
material_facts: The High Court had dictated its judgment but the transcript was not yet delivered as a judgment.
The matter was listed again after an issue concerning a deceased defendant was noticed, and the parties were allowed to address that issue before delivery.
issues.conclusion: The High Court's further hearing was permissible because the judgment had only been dictated and had not yet been delivered.
issues.legal_principle: The Court determined from the record that the judgment had been dictated but not delivered, and that the matter was listed again for further hearing before delivery. The Court therefore rejected the contention that the High Court had improperly reopened a concluded matter.

predicates.challenge_to_further_hearing: A party challenges a court's decision to hear further submissions after it has dictated a judgment.
predicates.judgment_dictated_but_not_delivered: The court has dictated its judgment but has not yet delivered it.
predicates.court_may_continue_hearing_before_delive: The court may continue hearing the matter before delivering its judgment.

issues.definition: If a judgment has been dictated but not delivered, the court may hear further submissions before delivery.
